---
title: "Covariates and the time grid"
---

The emulator takes twelve numbers. They describe the setting as it stands and the campaign
being evaluated. Everything the model knows about a district is in those twelve values.

## The twelve covariates

The names, and their canonical order, are carried in the checkpoint itself.

```{python}
from stateMINT.model import Mamba2Regressor

artifact = Mamba2Regressor.from_pretrained(
    "dide-ic/stateMINT", predictor="prevalence", revision="v1.2.2",
)

for i, name in enumerate(artifact.preprocessing_config["static_covars"], start=1):
    print(f"{i:2d}. {name}")
```

You pass them as a dictionary, one per scenario, so you do not have to reproduce the order
above. All twelve keys must be present.

| Covariate | Meaning | Range | Where it comes from |
|---|---|---|---|
| `eir` | Infectious bites per person per year | > 0, roughly 0.1–200 | [estiMINT](../04-estimint/estimating-eir.qmd), from a measured prevalence |
| `dn0_use` | Probability a mosquito dies on contact with a treated net, under the nets in place now | 0–0.56 | `calculate_dn0` on the current net mix ([Nets and dn0](../04-estimint/nets-and-dn0.qmd)) |
| `dn0_future` | The same probability, under the campaign net | 0–0.56 | `calculate_dn0` on the campaign net mix |
| `Q0` | Human blood index | 0–1, typically 0.7–0.95 | Vector species bionomics |
| `phi_bednets` | Share of bites taken while people are in bed | 0–1, typically 0.6–0.9 | Vector species bionomics |
| `seasonal` | Transmission profile. 0 perennial, 1 strongly seasonal | 0 or 1 | The setting |
| `routine` | Routine (continuous) net distribution running alongside the campaign | 0 or 1 | The campaign |
| `itn_use` | ITN coverage now | 0–1 | Survey or programme data |
| `irs_use` | IRS coverage now | 0–1 | Programme data |
| `itn_future` | ITN coverage from the campaign onwards | 0–1 | The campaign |
| `irs_future` | IRS coverage from the campaign onwards | 0–1 | The campaign |
| `lsm` | Larval source management coverage from the campaign onwards | 0–1 | The campaign |

`dn0_use` and `itn_use` describe the nets between them, and the emulator reads them as a pair.

Omitting a covariate is an error. The error names the ones you left out.

```{python}
covars = {
    "eir": 31.96, "dn0_use": 0.311, "dn0_future": 0.485,
    "Q0": 0.85, "phi_bednets": 0.80, "seasonal": 0,
    "routine": 0.0, "itn_use": 0.70, "irs_use": 0.0,
    "itn_future": 0.70, "irs_future": 0.0, "lsm": 0.0,
}

incomplete = {k: v for k, v in covars.items() if k != "lsm"}

try:
    artifact.predict([incomplete])
except ValueError as err:
    print(f"{type(err).__name__}: {err}")
```

## `_use` and `_future`

Three quantities appear twice. The `_use` suffix is the state of the world before the
campaign. The `_future` suffix is the campaign itself, in force from day 3285 onwards.

- `dn0_use` → `dn0_future`: the net product changes, so its lethality changes.
- `itn_use` → `itn_future`: the coverage the campaign achieves.
- `irs_use` → `irs_future`: spraying before, and spraying after.

`lsm` and `routine` have no `_use` counterpart, since they exist only as campaign quantities.

## The pre-campaign window

Five covariates (`dn0_future`, `itn_future`, `irs_future`, `lsm` and `routine`) are held
at zero for every timestep before the intervention day, whatever you pass. They take their
value only from day 3285 onwards.

```{python}
print(artifact.preprocessing_config["after_intervention"])
```

Two scenarios that are identical in the present and different in every campaign field have
feature matrices that are indistinguishable until the campaign starts.

```{python}
import numpy as np

withdraw = dict(covars, dn0_future=0.0, itn_future=0.0, irs_future=0.0, lsm=0.0, routine=0.0)
package  = dict(covars, dn0_future=0.55, itn_future=0.90, irs_future=0.60, lsm=0.30, routine=1.0)

X = artifact.prepare_inputs([withdraw, package])
identical = np.isclose(X[0], X[1]).all(axis=1)
first_difference = int(np.argmin(identical))

print(f"input shape          : {X.shape}")
print(f"rows identical to    : step {first_difference - 1}")
print(f"first differing step : {first_difference}")
print(f"identical before it  : {bool(identical[:first_difference].all())}")
```

So the emulator cannot represent a larviciding programme that has been running for years,
or a routine distribution channel that predates the campaign. Whatever you put in `lsm` or
`routine` begins at day 3285. The pre-campaign period is described entirely by `eir`,
`dn0_use`, `itn_use`, `irs_use`, `Q0`, `phi_bednets` and `seasonal`. If an existing
larviciding programme is depressing transmission, that suppression is already inside the
EIR you estimated from the observed prevalence.

::: {.callout-important}
## Future coverage

Leaving `itn_future` and `dn0_future` at zero does not mean *keep the nets as they are*. It
means *the nets are withdrawn from day 3285 onwards*. The same holds for `irs_future`. It does
not inherit `irs_use`.

To model an existing programme continuing you have to restate it, setting `itn_future` to the
coverage the campaign sustains and `dn0_future` to the lethality of the net it distributes.
The same trap has the same shape at the [`run_scenarios`](../06-scenarios/run-scenarios.qmd)
level. `net_type_future`, `itn_future` and `irs_future` all default to nothing, and a
`Scenario` that omits them is a scenario in which the intervention is withdrawn.

The failure is silent, and the result is a plausible trajectory of the wrong scenario.
:::

## The time grid

Nothing about the axis is passed in. The emulator reconstructs it from four numbers in the
checkpoint's preprocessing config, and they are worth reading out rather than hard-coding.

```{python}
cfg = artifact.preprocessing_config

n_steps          = cfg["n_steps"]
window_size      = cfg["window_size"]
model_start_day  = cfg["model_start_day"]
intervention_day = cfg["intervention_day"]

print(f"n_steps          = {n_steps}")
print(f"window_size      = {window_size} days")
print(f"model_start_day  = {model_start_day}")
print(f"intervention_day = {intervention_day}")
```

The simulation is run for longer than this. The first six years are burn-in and are
discarded. What survives is `n_steps` windows of `window_size` days, beginning at
`model_start_day`.

```{python}
abs_t = model_start_day + window_size * np.arange(n_steps)
years = (abs_t - intervention_day) / 365
idx_y9 = int(np.argmin(np.abs(abs_t - intervention_day)))

print(f"abs_t  : day {abs_t[0]} to day {abs_t[-1]}")
print(f"years  : {years[0]:+.2f} to {years[-1]:+.2f}")
print(f"idx_y9 : {idx_y9}  (day {abs_t[idx_y9]})")
```

`abs_t` is the absolute simulation day of each window, and `years` recentres it on the
campaign. That is the axis worth plotting against, negative before, positive after, and zero
the day the nets go out.

`idx_y9` is the index of the window nearest the campaign, the *ninth year* of the simulation.
That is where the name comes from, and where estiMINT's `prev_y9` is measured. At day 3282 it
is the last window before the switch, three days short of it.

Read the baseline off `idx_y9`, and check the emulator there against the prevalence you fed
the pipeline. Do not read it off the mean of the pre-campaign years. Day 2190 sits exactly
1095 days (three years) before the campaign, which is one mass-distribution cycle. The
baseline window opens on the previous net distribution and closes on the next one. It is not
a flat equilibrium, and its annual means are nowhere near `prev_y9`. The shape it has is
plotted in [Plotting trajectories](plotting.qmd).
